paragraphs.text: Lesson 15, where are you spending the holiday?
Listen to the conversation between co-workers Rhonda and Mac as you answer the comprehension
questions.
Man, I cannot wait for this week to end and for Thanksgiving to begin.
If I see one more report, I'm going to pull my hair out.
This has really been the week from hell.
Mr. Green sure piles on the work every time we prepare to take off for a holiday.
That's because he's a tightwad.
It wouldn't be the end of the world if he allowed his employees to have a few paid days off.
That's why he's made this last week so tough.
He wants to squeeze out the productivity before the holiday.
Surprise he hasn't chained us to our desks yet.
I know, but let's not let him ruin our Thanksgiving.
When I get out of this stuffy office, I'm going straight to the grocery store and buying
the biggest turkey I can find, along with the ingredients to make one of my homemade pumpkin
pies.
Oh, now my mouth is watering.
As much as I love my wife, she can't cook to save her life.
We usually spend our Thanksgiving meal at a restaurant.
In fact, I can't remember the last time I actually had some homemade pumpkin pie.
Well, then why don't you load Megan and the kids into the car and come over to our house
on Thanksgiving.
We'd love to have you.
Oh, I don't know.
We wouldn't want to intrude on your family's holiday.
Who's intruding?
You guys are like family to us, Mac.
Intruding?
Good grief.
Alright, okay, we'll come.
Great.
We'll have a ball.
You just wait and see.
Roger will get the fireplace going.
We'll stuff ourselves full of turkey and pumpkin pie, save her some hot chocolate, and sit by
the fire.
Ah, that sounds really nice.
Way better than sitting in a plastic booth listening to some crabby waitress complaining
about working on Thanksgiving.
Sure puts a damper on my holiday spirit.
Well, keep in mind that we all have to make a living.
That waitress is probably just scraping by.
It is sad that some people can't be with their families on the holidays.
I feel bad for those people.
Like Mr. Green.
I don't think he has any family in the area.
He'll probably spend the holiday right here in the office pouring over reports and grumbling
that his accounting department is incompetent.
Maybe we should invite the old fart to Thanksgiving at my home?
You might want to think twice about that, Rhonda.
He's so demanding he'll probably write up a report critiquing your pumpkin pie and file
it with your performance review.
Don't be so uptight, Mac.
I'm sure even Mr. Green loosens up a bit during the holidays.
Yeah, I will invite him if he doesn't have any other plans.
The more the merrier I suppose.
Okay, I'm just going to wrap up a few things and then head home.
See you tomorrow at 6.
You bet.
Let's learn the vocabulary from Mac and Rhonda's conversation.
Mac says, if I see one more report, I'm going to pull my hair out.
This expression, I'm going to pull my hair out, is an exaggerated way to express that
you can't endure much more.
Rhonda says, Mr. Green sure piles on the work every time we prepare to take off for a holiday.
This phrasal verb, piles on the work means he gives lots of work.
Mac replies, that's because he's a tightwad.
A tightwad is someone who doesn't like to spend money.
It has a negative connotation, like someone who doesn't spend even when they really should
be more generous with their money.
Then Mac says, it wouldn't be the end of the world if he allowed his employees to have
a few paid days off.
It wouldn't be the end of the world means it wouldn't be a disaster.
Mac says that Mr. Green wants to squeeze out the productivity before the holiday.
Squeeze out means to get something by applying pressure.
And finally Mac says, I'm surprised he hasn't chained us to our desks yet.
The word chained means used metal chains to keep someone prisoner.
Rhonda replies, I know, but let's not let him ruin our Thanksgiving.
The word ruin is a verb meaning destroy or make bad.
Then Rhonda says what she's going to do after she gets out of this stuffy office.
The word stuffy describes a place that lacks ventilation.
It has a negative connotation.
It's usually unpleasant to be in a stuffy place.
When Rhonda describes what she's planning to make for Thanksgiving, Mac says, oh, now
my mouth is watering.
My mouth is watering means that sounds delicious.
I want to eat it.
And Mac adds, as much as I love my wife, she can't cook to save her life.
This expression means she has zero cooking ability.
So Rhonda invites Mac and his wife and kids to spend Thanksgiving at her house.
Mac is initially hesitant.
He says, oh, I don't know.
We wouldn't want to intrude on your family's holiday.
The verb intrude means to enter without permission or without being welcome.
But Rhonda says she considers Mac and his family to be like family to her.
She says, intruding, good grief.
Good grief is an exclamation of surprise, shock, or amazement.
So Rhonda is surprised that Mac would feel like he was intruding because apparently the
two families are quite close friends.
So Mac agrees to come.
And Rhonda says, great, we'll have a ball.
Have a ball means have fun, have a good time.
It's just another expression similar to have a blast.
Rhonda says that on Thanksgiving, we'll stuff ourselves full of turkey and pumpkin pie.
Stuff ourselves means to eat excessively.
When you've eaten too much, you can say, I'm stuffed instead of I'm full.
I'm stuffed means I'm completely full.
I've eaten too much and I can't eat another bite.
Rhonda also says, we'll savor some hot chocolate and sit by the fire.
The word savor means to greatly appreciate the taste or smell of something.
When you're eating or drinking something, you take the time to really enjoy it.
That is what savor means.
Mac replies, that sounds really nice.
Way better than sitting in a plastic booth listening to some crabby waitress complaining.
The word booth refers to a type of seating used in diners and restaurants.
A booth is like a long bench with a back instead of individual chairs.
The word crabby means in a bad mood.
So Mac is saying that when he goes to a restaurant on Thanksgiving, the waitress is usually crabby.
She's in a bad mood because she has to work on the holiday.
Then he says, it sure puts a damper on my holiday spirit.
The expression puts a damper on means it makes something less enjoyable.
Rhonda reminds Mac, well, keep in mind that we all have to make a living.
Keep in mind means remember or don't forget.
She says, that waitress is probably just scraping by.
The phrasal verb scraping by means having difficulty surviving on a low salary.
Rhonda feels bad for people who can't spend Thanksgiving with their families, and Mac points out that Mr. Green doesn't have any family in the area.
He says, he'll probably spend the holiday right here in the office pouring over reports.
The phrasal verb pouring over means to read or look at something very carefully.
And Mac says that Mr. Green will be grumbling that his accounting department is incompetent.
The word grumbling means complaining in a low voice.
And incompetent means not intelligent, not skilled.
Rhonda then suggests, maybe we should invite the old fart thanksgiving at my home.
Old fart is a disrespectful way to refer to an older person.
This expression is very rude.
Mac says, you might want to think twice about that Rhonda.
To think twice about something means to reconsider if it is truly a good idea or not.
Mac says that Mr. Green is so demanding that he'll probably write up a report critiquing your pumpkin pie.
The word critiquing means analyzing and evaluating.
Critiquing is different from criticizing.
Criticizing means saying bad things.
But critiquing means analyzing and saying both bad things and good things.
But Rhonda says, don't be so uptight Mac.
Up tight means anxious or tense.
Rhonda continues, I'm sure even Mr. Green loosens up a bit during the holidays.
To loosen up means to become more relaxed and friendly.
And Rhonda decides that she will invite him.
Mac accepts her decision saying, the more the merrier I suppose.
This expression, the more the merrier means if there are more people it will be more fun or more enjoyable.
Then Mac says, okay, I'm just going to wrap up a few things.
Wrap up means finish.
And after Mac wraps up his work he's going to go home.
He says to Rhonda, see you tomorrow at 6, and Rhonda replies, you bet.
You bet means yes, definitely.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
